interview_metadata.name: Maria Buendia
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Okay, where do I start. I was born in Guanajuato, Mexico, and my family brought me to the States when I was real little, like five or six. We settled in Norcross first, then my dad found steadier work with a landscaping crew and we moved over to Lilburn. Growing up it was Spanish at home, English at school, and a lot of back and forth at church. My mom worked cleaning houses and my dad did yard work for bigger houses in Dunwoody, so they were gone a lot. I'm the oldest of four, so from maybe ten years old I was heating up tortillas, changing diapers, signing permission slips my parents couldn't read. I liked school, especially art class and anything where I could use my hands, but I left in eleventh grade when my mom had my youngest brother and got really sick after — somebody had to be home. I kept telling myself I'd go back, but then I met Hector at a quinceañera when I was eighteen, we got married at twenty-one in the church on Arcado, and we had our daughter Lupita a year later and our son Mateo three years after that. So my twenties were diapers, food stamps, helping Hector with his drywall business on paper, and running the kitchen for every baptism and birthday on our block. Somewhere in there the church lady Doña Rosa pulled me into planning the parish festival, and that just — it unlocked something. I've been doing community stuff ever since. Last year I started helping out at the Lilburn School of the Arts with their Latino programming, and I'm finally studying for my GED on a laptop we got refurbished from the library. That's the short version, anyway.

follow_ups.question: You mentioned Doña Rosa pulling you in — what was that first festival like?
follow_ups.response: Oh, it was a disaster and I loved it. This was Our Lady of Guadalupe's feast day, December of 2013 I think, and she just handed me the food tent because nobody else would do it. I had like sixty pounds of masa, three abuelas who didn't agree on anything, and a broken warmer. But we fed three hundred people and I realized I was good at keeping everyone calm. Doña Rosa told me afterward, 'mija, you're an organizer, not a cook,' and I cried in my car.

follow_ups.question: What does Hector do now, and how's his work going?
follow_ups.response: He's still in drywall and light framing, mostly subcontracting for a guy named Beto out of Tucker. Work comes and goes with the weather and the housing market. Right now it's okay, he's on a job in Suwanee that's gonna run through summer.

follow_ups.question: Leaving school in eleventh grade — how do you feel about that now?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, some days I'm fine with it because my family needed me. Other days, especially when I'm filling out paperwork at the arts center and I see 'highest degree' on the form, it stings. That's why the GED matters to me. I want to check that box.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yeah, I'd say when I was twenty-six. I had just had Mateo, and a lady from the church, Sister Annette, she told me about a scholarship through Gwinnett Tech for pastry arts. Full tuition, childcare stipend, the works. I had the application filled out, I had the letters. And the same week Hector's truck transmission went, my mom got diagnosed with diabetes — the bad kind where she was losing feeling in her feet — and Lupita started kindergarten and had separation stuff. I sat at the kitchen table with that envelope for like three days. I ended up not mailing it. Instead I doubled down on the church events and took over the Christmas tamale sale, which that year raised almost four thousand dollars for the youth group. So I didn't become a pastry chef. But I became the person people call when they need something organized. I think about that envelope a lot. I don't regret it, exactly, but I wonder.

follow_ups.question: Do you still have the application?
follow_ups.response: I do actually. It's in a folder in my filing cabinet with the kids' birth certificates. I pull it out sometimes when I'm feeling stuck.

follow_ups.question: Has Sister Annette stayed in your life?
follow_ups.response: She passed in 2021, COVID. That was hard. She was the first person outside my family who told me I was smart.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a choice. A painful one, but a choice. I weighed it out on a napkin — literally, I did the math on what we'd lose in hours if I was in class. It didn't pencil. I chose my family, eyes open.

follow_ups.question: Do you tell your kids about that decision?
follow_ups.response: I tell Lupita. She's fourteen now and she needs to know that choices cost something. I don't want her making mine.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yeah. If there was real childcare — not a stipend, actual care — I might have gone. And if somebody had helped Hector figure out his taxes earlier, we wouldn't have been so tight. The help was there in pieces but nobody connected them for us.

follow_ups.question: Who do you think should have connected the pieces?
follow_ups.response: Honestly? Somebody like me. That's what a community outreach coordinator does, and that's why I want that job.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: Yes, so it's me, Hector — he's my husband, we've been married thirteen years in October — and our two kids, Lupita who just turned fourteen, and Mateo who's eleven. My parents Ramon and Esperanza live about twelve minutes away off Killian Hill Road, and my three younger siblings are scattered — my sister Adriana is in Duluth with her three kids, my brother Javier is a diesel mechanic out near Buford, and my youngest brother Tomás is finishing up his associate's at Georgia State Perimeter, he still lives with my parents. My mother-in-law Flor is in Monterrey and we video-call her every Sunday after mass. Family for me is big — I've got cousins in Norcross and Snellville I see monthly at least. My compadres Rogelio and Maricela are basically family too, they're Lupita's godparents. And Doña Rosa's daughter Cristina, she's my closest friend, we talk every day.

follow_ups.question: Who do you lean on most day-to-day?
follow_ups.response: Cristina and my mom. Cristina for venting, my mom for child logistics. If Mateo has a stomachache at school, it's Mom who picks him up because I don't drive yet — I mean, I drive, but I failed the test twice and haven't gone back.

follow_ups.question: Tell me more about Lupita.
follow_ups.response: She's something else. Quiet like her dad but sharp. She's in ninth grade at Berkmar, plays clarinet in marching band, and she draws these anime portraits that are — they're good. She sold a commission for twenty bucks to a classmate last month and I nearly cried.

follow_ups.question: And Mateo?
follow_ups.response: Mateo is a tornado. Soccer, fútbol, soccer, fútbol. He's on a rec league at Lilburn City Park and he'll be the kid who eats dinner in his cleats if I let him.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My abuela Consuelo — my dad's mom — is still alive in Guanajuato, she's 89. We send money every month and call on her birthday. I haven't seen her in person in almost nine years, which eats at me.

follow_ups.question: How much do you send?
follow_ups.response: A hundred fifty through Ria. Sometimes two hundred if there's a doctor visit.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Cristina I mentioned. Then there's my book club — six of us, we've been meeting monthly for almost four years at each other's houses. That's Cristina, Patricia who's a librarian at the Lilburn branch, Keisha who teaches fifth grade at Camp Creek, Fatima who just moved from Egypt two years ago, Dolores who's Puerto Rican and retired, and Jessamyn who runs her own photography business. I also got close with Ms. Deborah at the arts center — she's my actual mentor there. And my yoga people — I go Tuesday and Thursday mornings at Twisted Noodle Yoga downtown, there's a little regulars group.

follow_ups.question: What's the book club reading now?
follow_ups.response: We just finished Pachinko by Min Jin Lee. Before that was The House of the Spirits for the third time, because Dolores insisted, and she was right.

follow_ups.question: How'd you meet Ms. Deborah?
follow_ups.response: She came to our parish festival in 2023 looking for Latino community partners and I was the one who cornered her at the taco stand. She hired me as a paid contractor three months later.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We're in Lilburn, kind of between Old Town and Five Forks, in a little subdivision called Hillside Oaks — townhomes, built in the nineties. It's mixed — Latino families, Korean families, some Black families, a few older white couples who've been here since it was built. Our next-door neighbors the Parks run a dry cleaner and we watch each other's packages. The elementary school Mateo went to, Camp Creek Elementary, is walking distance, which was huge. The Korean grocery H-Mart and the Mexican market El Bodegón are both less than ten minutes. Stone Mountain is twenty minutes if we want a hike. It's not fancy but it works and we've got roots here.

follow_ups.question: How long have you been in that subdivision?
follow_ups.response: Nine years in this townhouse. We rented in an apartment off Pleasant Hill before that.

follow_ups.question: What do you love most about the area?
follow_ups.response: Honestly? That my kids are growing up hearing Spanish, Korean, Vietnamese, and English on the same block. They think that's normal, and I love that.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: Mostly safe. We've had a few car break-ins in our row, and there was a scary thing at the 7-Eleven on Lawrenceville Highway last year. I lock everything. I don't walk after dark alone. But I let the kids ride bikes on the cul-de-sac, so, yeah. Safe enough.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a Ring or anything like that?
follow_ups.response: We got a Ring doorbell for Christmas from my brother Javier. Hector grumbled but he checks it more than anyone.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: Ups — community, the church, schools aren't bad, close to family. Downs — traffic on 29 is terrible, our HOA is a pain about every little thing, and the property taxes went up two years in a row. Feels like Lilburn is changing, getting more expensive. But I'm not going anywhere.

follow_ups.question: What HOA thing bugs you most?
follow_ups.response: They cited us for the vegetable garden in the front bed. I moved it to the back but I'm still salty.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Just the four of us — me, Hector, Lupita, and Mateo. My brother Tomás crashes on our couch maybe one weekend a month when my parents' house gets crowded, but he doesn't live here. Oh, and our dog Paco, a chihuahua mix we rescued from the Humane Society two years ago. He thinks he owns the place.

follow_ups.question: Any other pets?
follow_ups.response: A betta fish Mateo named Ronaldo. And the plants, which Hector calls pets.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: All four of us are permanent.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Just Tomás occasionally, like I said. And my niece Gaby slept over last Friday.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody like that.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Monday through Friday I'm up at 5:45 to pack lunches — Hector takes his at 6:30. Kids are up at 6:45, on the bus by 7:30. Tuesdays and Thursdays I hit the 9 AM yoga class at Twisted Noodle. Mondays and Wednesdays I'm at the arts center from 10 to 3 — that's my contract hours. Fridays I clean, cook for Sunday, and do GED work on Khan Academy. Saturdays rotate — soccer game for Mateo, grocery run to El Bodegón and Aldi, maybe an event I'm helping run. Sundays are church at 10, big family lunch at my parents' at 1, and whatever school stuff's due Monday. I wind down around 10 PM with a telenovela or a book.

follow_ups.question: Which telenovela are you on?
follow_ups.response: I'm on Vencer el Pasado reruns. Don't judge me.

follow_ups.question: How does Hector's schedule mesh with yours?
follow_ups.response: He's gone 6:30 to 5:30 most weekdays. Saturdays he sometimes works too. So honestly the mornings and Sundays are our real together time.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: Officially I'm what they call 'no occupation' on the census, meaning I don't have a W-2 full-time job. But I work. I do contract work for the Lilburn School of the Arts as a Latino community liaison, about ten to fifteen hours a week at $18 an hour, which comes out to maybe $700-900 a month depending. I also get paid $50 to $200 to plan baptisms and quinceañeras for families in the parish — maybe two a month. And I help Hector with his invoicing and receipts, which isn't paid but it keeps us afloat. I'm also in school for my GED, so that's unpaid work I do on me.

follow_ups.question: How does the arts center pay you — check, 1099?
follow_ups.response: 1099. Which is why taxes last year were a nightmare and I had to pay in $340 I didn't expect.

follow_ups.question: When did you start the arts center work?
follow_ups.response: September 2023. So a little over two years.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I moderate two Facebook groups — Lilburn Moms en Español, about 800 members, and Ballet Folklórico de Gwinnett, smaller, about 150. That takes an hour a day easy. I also help my parents with their mail and any English paperwork — Medicare, utility stuff, that kind of thing. And I'm on the rotating potluck chain for the book club, so once every six weeks I'm hosting seven women in my living room.

follow_ups.question: What's the hardest moderator situation you've had?
follow_ups.response: Last year a woman was selling a 'miracle diet tea' in Lilburn Moms en Español and people were buying it. I had to research it, post a notice, and ban her. She emailed me nasty stuff for a week.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Two big ones. First, I started GED prep in January — that's two evenings a week plus weekends. Second, my folk-dance troupe, Ballet Folklórico Fuerza Latina, started practicing twice a week instead of once because we have a big performance at the Atlanta Latin American Festival in July. So my Wednesdays are now yoga-morning, arts-center-afternoon, folklórico-evening. It's a lot.

follow_ups.question: How's the GED going?
follow_ups.response: Math is kicking my butt. Reading I'm crushing. Science I'm somewhere in the middle.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: Both kids get on the Gwinnett County bus at 7:30. Lupita's at Berkmar High, gets home at 3:45. She's got marching band practice Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays till 5:30 in the fall, then art club Tuesdays. Mateo's at Camp Creek Middle, home at 4:10. He's got soccer practice Tuesdays and Thursdays at the park, games Saturdays. Homework from like 4 to 6, dinner at 6:30, showers, reading, bed by 9 for Mateo and 10 for Lupita. Screens go off at 8:30 on school nights.

follow_ups.question: Do they help with dinner or chores?
follow_ups.response: Lupita folds laundry and makes rice. Mateo sets the table and walks Paco. They both fight about the dishwasher.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: A few. Mostly traffic — Hector got pulled over maybe four times in the last ten years, once for a taillight, once for supposedly rolling a stop, and a couple random ones that didn't feel random to us. I got a speeding ticket in 2019 that took me months to pay off. And there was one time around 2017 when Gwinnett County deputies came to a neighbor's apartment for a domestic call and knocked on ours by mistake at 1 AM — that shook us up. We had the kids in our bed for a week after.

follow_ups.question: How do you feel about the Gwinnett County police overall?
follow_ups.response: Mixed. Some officers have been kind. But the 287(g) stuff during the Sheriff Conway years really scared our community. I'm glad that ended.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: When I helped organize the parish Noche Buena event in 2022, we had to coordinate with a police officer for traffic. He was actually great — bilingual, respectful, let the kids sit in his cruiser. That was a good one.

follow_ups.question: Do you know any officers personally?
follow_ups.response: Just Officer Ramirez from that event. And Cristina's cousin is on the Norcross force.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: My cousin Beto — different Beto than Hector's boss — got picked up on a DUI in 2018 and did thirty days. It was a mess for his family. Nobody in my immediate family has been arrested.

follow_ups.question: How did that affect your extended family?
follow_ups.response: His wife nearly lost their apartment. My mom and I made sure she had groceries every week until he got out.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in every general and every midterm. I became a citizen in 2016 — that was one of the proudest days of my life — and I've voted in every election since. Local too, school board, county commission. I don't always vote in primaries, honestly, because I get confused by the rules in Georgia about which primary I can pick. But generals, yes, always.

follow_ups.question: Where do you vote?
follow_ups.response: At the Lilburn Activity Building. Usually on the first Saturday of early voting — I bring Lupita with me so she sees it.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I'd call myself a moderate Democrat, probably. Maybe center-left. I care about immigration reform — obviously, given my family — and I believe in strong public schools, Medicaid expansion, and a living wage. I voted for Biden in 2020 and Harris in 2024. But I'm not where some of my younger cousins are on everything. I'm Catholic, so abortion is hard for me personally — I think it should stay legal but I'd never have one myself, and I don't like how the debate gets flattened. On guns I'm more liberal than my husband; he wants a pistol in the nightstand, I don't. On the border, I'm honestly complicated — I think the current system is cruel and doesn't work, but I also don't think 'open borders' is realistic or fair to people who waited like my family did. On race and policing, I lean progressive. On trans stuff, I'm still figuring it out but I land on 'be kind, let people be.' On taxes, I think rich people should pay more and working families like mine should pay less. The party label matters less to me than whether someone gets what it's like to make $35,000 a year in Georgia.

follow_ups.question: Anybody you really admire in politics?
follow_ups.response: Stacey Abrams, even though she lost. And my county commissioner Marlene Fosque — she showed up at our Día de los Muertos event in 2022 and actually talked to people.

follow_ups.question: Anyone you really don't like?
follow_ups.response: I'm gonna be diplomatic and say the ones who use immigrants as a punching bag. You know who they are.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I've gotten more skeptical of both parties, actually. I used to be pretty reliably blue-no-matter-who. But the way Democrats talk about Latinos like we're one bloc annoys me — we're not. Some of my cousins voted Trump in 2024 and I disagreed with them but I understand why: they own small businesses, inflation hurt them, and they feel Democrats didn't show up. At the same time, I've gotten more progressive on economic stuff — housing costs, childcare, the way tipped workers get screwed. So I'm more nuanced than I was five years ago. Less team-sports about it.

follow_ups.question: What did 2024 feel like for you?
follow_ups.response: Exhausting. I worked two voter registration drives at the church and we registered 140 people, which I'm proud of. But the results were hard and my family group chat was ugly for about two weeks.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: Affected me somewhat. I'm Latina, so my experience with policing is different from Black folks' — we have overlap and we have differences. I went to one march in Decatur in June 2020, with Cristina and Keisha. I've read more books on race since then — White Rage, The Warmth of Other Suns, I'm in the middle of Caste now. It made me think harder about what I teach my kids about police. I tell Mateo to always keep his hands visible, speak respectfully, don't argue — same as my dad told me. Some of that advice feels different now than it did ten years ago.

follow_ups.question: Has the book club talked about BLM?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a lot. Keisha especially has been patient with our questions. We read How to Be an Antiracist in 2021.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core demand — that Black people should not die at routine police encounters — is just basic. I don't think 'defund the police' as a slogan was strategically smart, but I understand what was meant. What I struggle with is how to be a good ally without centering myself. I try to listen more than talk, support Black-owned businesses — there's a bakery in Stone Mountain I go to every month — and speak up when my Latino relatives say anti-Black things, which happens more than I wish it did.

follow_ups.question: Is there tension in your family on this?
follow_ups.response: Yeah. My Tio Roberto says things I have to correct. It's uncomfortable but I do it, especially around my kids.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think we're in a backlash period. Schools banning books, affirmative action gone, the rhetoric getting uglier. I worry for my kids. Mateo is dark-skinned and already hears jokes at school. Lupita is lighter and navigates it differently. I talk to them about being proud of being Mexican-American and about understanding that our Blackness or whiteness or in-between-ness shapes how people treat us, whether we like it or not.

follow_ups.question: Has Mateo told you about specific incidents?
follow_ups.response: A kid called him the n-word on the bus in December. I met with the principal. It got handled but Mateo was shaken for weeks.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: Mix. I marched once in 2020. I've had hard conversations with family, including my dad. I've moderated my Facebook groups around these topics. I donated to the Bail Project once. I'm not an activist but I'm not silent either.

follow_ups.question: Would you march again?
follow_ups.response: Yes, if the moment called for it and I could bring the kids safely.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Varies. Cristina is more progressive than me and pushes me. Keisha, being Black, has her own experience and has been generous in sharing it. Hector thinks a lot about it but doesn't talk publicly — he saw a lot of colorism in construction. My parents are of the generation where they just want to keep their heads down; my mom especially. My younger siblings are all over the map.

follow_ups.question: What does Hector say when he does talk?
follow_ups.response: He told me once that on his crews, white guys get the foreman spot first, then light-skinned Latinos, then everyone else. He's just stating facts.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall decent. I'm 34, I'm in the biggest pair of jeans I've ever worn — I'm maybe 35 pounds heavier than I'd like to be. I have borderline hypertension, which my doctor says is from salt and stress, and I had gestational diabetes with both pregnancies, so I'm at high risk for Type 2 like my mom. I do yoga twice a week, walk with the dog, try to eat more vegetables. My cholesterol was a little high last panel. I don't smoke. I drink socially, maybe one or two drinks at a birthday or wedding. My teeth need work — I haven't been to a dentist in four years because of cost.

follow_ups.question: Who's your primary care doctor?
follow_ups.response: Dr. Chen at Gwinnett Community Clinic. She's on a sliding scale. I've been seeing her for six years.

follow_ups.question: What medications are you on?
follow_ups.response: Just a daily multivitamin and occasional ibuprofen. No prescriptions.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Hard: time, money, stress, and the fact that every celebration in my culture revolves around food. Easy: yoga is a real anchor, I can cook healthy when I plan, and Hector and the kids will usually eat what I cook. I have a Fitbit Hector got me for Mother's Day that I actually use.

follow_ups.question: What's your step goal?
follow_ups.response: 8,000. I hit it about four days a week.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Two things. I sprained my right ankle badly at folklórico practice in August 2024 and was in a boot for six weeks. And my hypertension got flagged at my annual in February 2025 — blood pressure was 142 over 90. Doctor wanted to put me on lisinopril, I asked for three months to try lifestyle first, and I brought it down to 128 over 82 last checkup. No broken bones, thank God. Some lower back pain I think is from carrying kids for years.

follow_ups.question: How'd you sprain your ankle?
follow_ups.response: Missed a step on a zapateado. Full commitment, full stupidity.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: The ankle thing cost me two events at the arts center. And when I have bad cramps — I get them monthly, doctor says possible endometriosis, we haven't pursued a diagnosis — I sometimes can't get out of bed for a day.

follow_ups.question: Why not pursue the endometriosis diagnosis?
follow_ups.response: The specialist visit was $400 up front plus imaging. I couldn't swing it.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: My mom's diabetes is the biggest ongoing thing. She's Type 2 with neuropathy. I go to her appointments when I can, manage her glucose log, and cook diabetic-friendly food for Sundays. Last year she had a diabetic ulcer on her foot that took four months to heal. Scared us. And Hector threw out his back in 2023 doing drywall — he was out of work five weeks.

follow_ups.question: How did you handle the five weeks Hector was out?
follow_ups.response: Savings got drained, we did a GoFundMe Cristina set up that raised $1,800, and my brother Javier paid our electric bill one month without asking.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: Oh yes. My teeth. My possible endometriosis. Hector's knees — he's needed an MRI for two years. The kids have Peach Care Georgia so they're covered, thank God. Hector and I are on a cheap ACA bronze plan with a $7,500 deductible, which basically means catastrophic only. Every checkup is out of pocket. I've done payment plans on three different bills.

follow_ups.question: Did you qualify for Medicaid expansion when Georgia rolled out Pathways?
follow_ups.response: We tried. Pathways requires 80 hours of verified work and the paperwork was impossible for Hector's 1099 income. We got denied twice.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Yes, all the time. I go to a curandera named Doña Lupe in Norcross for limpias — cleansings — maybe twice a year, especially after stressful periods. My mom uses sábila — aloe — and manzanilla tea for everything. I did a temazcal sweat lodge once in 2022 and it was intense. I believe in it and in Western medicine both. They're not in conflict for me.

follow_ups.question: What did Doña Lupe charge?
follow_ups.response: $40 cash. Eggs, herbs, prayers. I feel ten pounds lighter after.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I don't smoke. I drink socially, like I said — a Modelo or a margarita at a party, maybe a glass of wine at book club. I've never used it to cope. I think watching my Tío Roberto drink himself into problems in my twenties kind of inoculated me.

follow_ups.question: Does Hector drink?
follow_ups.response: He'll have two or three beers on a Friday after work, Coronas usually. Never more. He's pretty disciplined about it.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: No prescriptions for coping. I tried a THC gummy once at my friend Jessamyn's bachelorette in 2022 and I didn't love it — felt disconnected. I stick to yoga, prayer, and talking to Cristina when I'm spiraling. I take ibuprofen for cramps. That's really it.

follow_ups.question: Is marijuana common in your social circle?
follow_ups.response: A few people partake. It's legal-adjacent here and my younger cousins use it. I just don't.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: ACA bronze plan for Hector and me, $412 a month with subsidy. Kids on Peach Care, no premium. Sliding scale clinic for primary care. Free clinic off Indian Trail for dental emergencies — I haven't gone for routine stuff in years. We have maybe $900 in a health savings envelope. We cope, barely. One ER visit would wreck us.

follow_ups.question: Do you have life insurance?
follow_ups.response: Hector has a $50K term policy through an agent at church. I have $15K. Not enough but it's something.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I'm pro-vaccine. Kids have all their shots, I got COVID vaccines three times including the updated one in fall 2024, and my flu shot every October at CVS. My mom was hesitant but I got her boosted.

follow_ups.question: Any vaccine hesitancy in your circle?
follow_ups.response: Some. A couple of moms in my Facebook group went sideways on COVID. I didn't ban them, but I moderated the misinformation.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: Dr. Chen first. Then the CDC website, which I actually read in Spanish sometimes. NPR. My cousin Valeria who's a nurse at Gwinnett Medical. I don't trust random Facebook posts or WhatsApp forwards from my tías — those are a menace.

follow_ups.question: How do you correct WhatsApp misinformation?
follow_ups.response: Gently, and with a link from the CDC en español. Sometimes I lose the argument. Sometimes I win.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Mixed. Overall I'd say pretty good, more purposeful than I've felt in years. The arts center work is fulfilling. GED prep is hard but hopeful. My kids are healthy. My marriage is solid. But I've had stretches of anxiety, especially around money and around the election in November. I had a couple weeks in January where I didn't sleep well and snapped at Hector over dumb stuff. My mom's health worries are a constant low-grade hum. And honestly, the political climate has me on edge about our community. I've cried in the car three or four times this year, which for me is a lot.

follow_ups.question: What helps you reset?
follow_ups.response: Yoga. Prayer. A long walk with Paco. Or honestly, baking — I made pan de muerto three times in October and it was cheaper than therapy.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: November 2024, after the election. I'd worked so hard on voter registration and I felt crushed — not just because of who won, but because I felt like Latino voters were being blamed and caricatured from every direction. I sat in the parish parking lot one Wednesday after a meeting and just sobbed for twenty minutes. Then I wiped my face, drove to El Bodegón, bought ingredients for pozole, and fed twelve people at my house that Sunday. That's how I process.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk to anyone about it?
follow_ups.response: Cristina. And Father Miguel at confession the next week. He was kind.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have generalized anxiety. Diagnosed? No, never formally. But I know myself. I have periods where my chest is tight for no reason, I can't sleep, I ruminate. I think I had postpartum depression after Mateo that nobody caught — I was in a fog for about six months. I've never been on meds for mental health. I'd consider it but the stigma in my family is real and I haven't crossed that line.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever seen a therapist?
follow_ups.response: No. Cost and stigma. I journal instead. And I talk to Cristina, which is basically therapy.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: Hector deals with stress by going quiet. Lupita has some teenage anxiety — she started picking at her cuticles last year, which worries me. Mateo is a ball of energy, mostly fine. My mom has depression she won't name, tied to her diabetes.

follow_ups.question: Have you talked to Lupita about therapy?
follow_ups.response: I floated it. She said 'maybe.' I'm going to push on it this summer.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Very important. I'm Roman Catholic, raised in it, still in it. We go to Mass at Saint John Neumann most Sundays at 10 AM — it's the English Mass, though I'll sometimes go to the 12:30 Spanish Mass instead. I pray the rosary probably three times a week, not always out loud. I have a little altar in our bedroom with Our Lady of Guadalupe, a photo of my grandpa who passed, and a votive candle I light on his birthday. I volunteer with the parish festival committee and the youth group potlucks. I'd say my faith has gotten deeper in my thirties, not more rigid. I question things more. I don't agree with the Church on everything — I think women should be priests, I think the abortion discussion is more complicated than the hierarchy admits — but the community and the rhythms of the liturgical year are home.

follow_ups.question: Who's your priest?
follow_ups.response: Father Miguel Ramírez. He's been there seven years. He's a saint and a pain in my butt and I love him.

follow_ups.question: Do the kids go willingly?
follow_ups.response: Lupita is in her 'Mom I don't know what I believe' phase. Mateo loves the donuts after. We go as a family.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: Heavy Facebook user. Two moderator roles, probably two hours a day across posting, moderating, messaging. Instagram I use for the arts center mostly — I post event flyers and reels of folklórico practice. TikTok I scroll for maybe 30 minutes before bed, mostly recipe videos and dance videos. WhatsApp is where my actual family communication lives — three group chats, probably 200 messages a day total. I have Nextdoor for the neighborhood which I mostly ignore. I'm not on Twitter or X, and I deleted Snapchat years ago. YouTube for tutorials — pottery glazing, Excel for GED prep, that kind of thing.

follow_ups.question: What did you post on Instagram most recently?
follow_ups.response: A reel of the kids decorating eggs for Easter last Sunday, with a Selena soundtrack. 340 views, respectable.

follow_ups.question: What's your oldest Facebook friendship?
follow_ups.response: My cousin Valeria from like 2009. We went to middle school together.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: Financial, once — Cristina set up the GoFundMe I mentioned when Hector was hurt. Emotional, yes — I post vague stuff sometimes and my friends reach out. Book club DMs get real. I try not to overshare publicly though.

follow_ups.question: Would you do a GoFundMe yourself?
follow_ups.response: Only for someone else. I couldn't ask for myself. Pride, probably.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: Stress is up. Post-election, plus GED, plus folklórico performance prep, plus Mom's health. Coping — more yoga, less doomscrolling. I deleted the news app from my phone in December. I still get headlines once a day, that's it.

follow_ups.question: How's the phone limit working?
follow_ups.response: Shockingly well. I'm sleeping better.

transcript.question_text: This might be repetitive, but before we go on to the next section, I want to quickly make sure I have this right: who are you living with right now?
transcript.response: Me, Hector, Lupita, Mateo. Plus Paco the dog and Ronaldo the fish, but they don't count for your records.

transcript.question_text: Any babies or small children?
transcript.response: No, my youngest is eleven.

transcript.question_text: Anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Any lodgers, boarders, or employees who live here?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Who shares the responsibility for the rent, mortgage, or other household expenses?
transcript.response: Hector and me. We own the townhouse, mortgage is in both names.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to talk about how you make ends meet and what the monthly budget looks like for you and your family. What were your biggest expenses last month?
transcript.response: Mortgage is $1,485 with escrow. Health insurance $412. Utilities maybe $280 total. Groceries $900 — I track it. Gas two cars $260. Kids' activities and clothes $180. Car insurance $185. Phones $140. Internet $75. Church donation $100. That's the big stuff.

follow_ups.question: What's missing from that list?
follow_ups.response: Ria remittance to abuela, $150. Streaming, $30ish. Miscellaneous eating out, $120.

transcript.question_text: How much did your household spend in the past month? Is that the usual amount? And if not, how much do you usually spend and on what?
transcript.response: Last month we spent about $4,500. Usual is $4,200 to $4,500. Last month was higher because of taxes owed and Mateo's cleats. A normal month, $4,300ish.

follow_ups.question: What's the spendiest month of the year?
follow_ups.response: December. Christmas plus quinceañera season plus heating bills.

transcript.question_text: Does your household own or rent your home?
transcript.response: We own. Bought in 2017 for $178,000 with an FHA loan, 3.5% down from savings plus a gift from my mother-in-law. It's probably worth around $265,000 now, which is wild. About eighteen years left on the mortgage.

follow_ups.question: Have you refinanced?
follow_ups.response: We refinanced in 2020 when rates dropped. Saved us like $180 a month. Best financial move we ever made.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Summer electric spikes because of the AC — we hit $340 in July. December is Christmas plus heating, my mom's birthday, Posadas food, and we tithe extra. August is back-to-school clothes, supplies, fees — maybe $450 extra. May is dance recital costumes, folklórico dresses aren't cheap. Taxes hit in April with the 1099 stuff. And random stuff like the water heater in October, $850.

follow_ups.question: How do you plan for those spikes?
follow_ups.response: Envelope system. I keep an envelope per category and add $25-50 a month so it's there when needed.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: The water heater was rough. We put it on the Lowe's card at 0% for twelve months — I'm three payments into it. Mateo's cleats came out of the envelope. Taxes we had a little buffer for.

follow_ups.question: How do you feel about credit cards?
follow_ups.response: Useful if you don't carry a balance. I carry a balance sometimes. I'm not proud.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: I save. A savings account at Gwinnett Credit Union with about $2,400 in it — our emergency fund, which should be bigger. A Christmas club account with about $600 in it. Cash in an envelope in my dresser for unexpected stuff, maybe $300 right now. And I do a tanda — a rotating savings club — with seven women from church; I put in $100 a month and get $700 every seventh month.

follow_ups.question: What do you use the tanda for?
follow_ups.response: Big one-time things. Last payout went to the kids' back-to-school and one pottery class I treated myself to.

follow_ups.question: Retirement savings?
follow_ups.response: Almost nothing. Hector has a tiny IRA, maybe $3,200. I don't have anything formal. This worries me.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: Rainy day mostly. Plus a small bucket for a trip to Mexico in 2027 to see abuela — I've got $480 earmarked so far. We're also supposed to be saving for Lupita's quinceañera which is coming up in a year and a half, that's gonna be $4,000 minimum, and I've got maybe $700 toward it.

follow_ups.question: Is $4,000 a small quinceañera?
follow_ups.response: By our community standards, it's modest. Some families do $20,000. I want meaningful, not flashy.

transcript.question_text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you're paying on right now.
transcript.response: Mortgage $158,000 balance. Credit card, Chase, about $2,800 balance at 24% which is a mess I'm working on. Lowe's card $720 at 0% for another nine months. Car loan on Hector's truck, $9,400 at 6.2%, about two years left. No student loans — I never made it to college.

follow_ups.question: What's your plan for the Chase card?
follow_ups.response: I'm doing the snowball. $200 a month minimum, more when I can. Should be gone in 15 months.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven't had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.
transcript.response: January of this year. Arts center paid me late — administrative delay, three weeks late — and I had to delay the internet bill by ten days, pay a late fee. Also skipped a dentist cleaning I'd scheduled for myself. In November I borrowed $300 from my brother Javier for Thanksgiving stuff, paid him back December 15.

follow_ups.question: Did you tell Hector?
follow_ups.response: Yes. We're transparent on money, even when it's ugly.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Formally I'm classified as no occupation — homemaker. In practice I'm a contract community liaison at the Lilburn School of the Arts and a freelance event planner for families. At the arts center, my duties are: recruit Latino families for classes and events, translate materials from English to Spanish and back, host two monthly bilingual community gatherings, advise the director on culturally appropriate programming, and coordinate our annual Día de los Muertos festival which drew 800 people last year. For freelance events, I plan quinceañeras, baptisms, bridal showers, and birthday parties — I handle venue, menu, rentals, decor, and sometimes coordinate the mariachi. I also manage Hector's business paperwork: invoicing, mileage logs, tax prep. And I moderate two Spanish-language Facebook groups as part of community engagement.

follow_ups.question: How'd you learn event planning?
follow_ups.response: By doing. Parish festivals, family quinceañeras, trial and error. I read a library book on Excel in 2019 and it changed my life.

follow_ups.question: What's the best event you've planned?
follow_ups.response: My niece Gaby's quinceañera in October 2024. 140 people, under budget, three food stations, one dance that made my tía cry. I still dream about it.

transcript.question_text: Was your occupation covered by a union or employee association contract?
transcript.response: No, nothing like that. I'm a 1099 contractor.

follow_ups.question: Do you think you should be?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, gig workers deserve protections. But nobody's unionizing part-time arts contractors in Lilburn.

transcript.question_text: In the past year, how many weeks did you work (for a few hours, including paid vacation, paid sick leave, and military service)?
transcript.response: Paid work? Probably 48 of 52 weeks. I took off the week of Christmas and a week in July when the kids went to my parents'.

transcript.question_text: How many hours each week did you usually work?
transcript.response: Arts center about 12 hours, freelance events vary wildly — some weeks 0, some weeks 25. Average maybe 18 hours total paid.

transcript.question_text: In the past week, did you work for pay (even for 1 hour) at a job or business?
transcript.response: Yes, about 14 hours at the arts center plus three hours planning a baptism for the Delgado family.

transcript.question_text: Did you have more than one job or business, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: Yes — arts center contract plus freelance event planning. Two streams.

transcript.question_text: Now, in the past month, how many jobs did you work, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: Two — the arts center and freelance events. I did two events this past month, a baptism and a first-birthday party.

transcript.question_text: For your job or occupations, how much money did you receive in the past month?
transcript.response: Arts center, $864 last month — 48 hours at $18. Events, $350 combined. So $1,214.

transcript.question_text: How often do you get paid?
transcript.response: Arts center pays monthly via direct deposit, usually the 15th. Event clients pay day-of or within the week, cash or Zelle.

transcript.question_text: In total, how much did your household make in the past month?
transcript.response: Hector brought home about $3,800 after taxes — he had a good month. Plus my $1,214. So about $5,014 last month.

follow_ups.question: Is that typical?
follow_ups.response: Typical is $4,600 to $5,000. Slower months we've seen $3,800.

transcript.question_text: Switching gears a bit, let's talk a little about tax time. Did you file taxes last year (the most recent year)?
transcript.response: Yes, filed joint. We used TurboTax Self-Employed because of Hector's 1099 and my 1099. Owed $340 federal, got $190 state back. Paid H&R Block once in 2021 and never again — too expensive.

follow_ups.question: Did you claim EITC?
follow_ups.response: Yes, we get the Earned Income Tax Credit. It's meaningful for us, about $2,100.

transcript.question_text: Tell me more about your workplace. How long have you been at your current job? How would you describe the benefits that come with your job? (This could include things like health benefits, paid time off, vacation, and sick time.)
transcript.response: Arts center, since September 2023. Benefits: zero. No health, no PTO, no sick. 1099 life.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your relationships at work? (How is your relationship with your manager or boss? How are your relationships with your coworkers?)
transcript.response: Ms. Deborah, the director, is great — she trusts me, pays me on time usually. Coworkers are mostly volunteers and part-timers, I get along with all of them. The pottery teacher Javier can be moody but I like him.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about how predictable your work schedule is. How would you describe your job in terms of flexibility with your hours?
transcript.response: Arts center is flexible — I set my own hours within a weekly target. That's huge for me with kids. Events are unpredictable; you don't know if a client is gonna call Tuesday asking for a Saturday event. Sometimes I say no. The flip side is I can shift things for Lupita's band concert or if my mom needs me.

follow_ups.question: Would you give up flexibility for a W-2?
follow_ups.response: For the right job, yes. Benefits and a steady check would be life-changing. Depends on the hours.

transcript.question_text: Some people say it's hard to take or keep a job because of child care. How about for you?
transcript.response: Yes, huge factor. My parents are my childcare backup. Without them I couldn't do what I do. That's why I've never pursued a full-time office job.

transcript.question_text: Do you receive any payments or benefits from SNAP, food stamps, housing voucher payments, supplemental security income, or any other programs like that?
transcript.response: We got SNAP in 2013-2016 when the kids were little. Not now. Kids are on Peach Care. I do use WIC info for a family I help at church but we don't qualify ourselves anymore. No housing vouchers, no SSI.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about times over the last year when your income was especially low. And tell me about all the things you did to make ends meet during that time.
transcript.response: February was slow — only one event, and the arts center was closed for a week for renovation. Income dropped to maybe $750. I pulled from the emergency fund, skipped an eye doctor appointment, and did a big bean-and-rice push for groceries. Cristina brought us tamales, which helped more than she knows.

follow_ups.question: Did you apply for any assistance?
follow_ups.response: No, we don't qualify for most things because of Hector's income on paper. We're in the gap.

transcript.question_text: What would it be like for you if you had to spend $400 for an emergency? Would you have the money, and if not, how would you get it?
transcript.response: I'd have it. It'd drain the emergency fund dangerously but I'd have it. If it were $1,500, I'd struggle — probably credit card plus borrow from Javier.

follow_ups.question: How does it feel to be asked that?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, grateful that the answer is yes now. Five years ago it was no.

transcript.question_text: Overall, how do you feel about your financial situation?
transcript.response: Cautiously okay. We own our house. We eat well. Our kids have what they need. We don't take vacations beyond Savannah or Pigeon Forge. We don't have retirement savings worth mentioning. We're one medical emergency or one truck failure from real trouble. But we're more stable than my parents were at our age. I look at my budget spreadsheet — yes I have a spreadsheet — and I feel in control most days. Getting my GED, getting to a W-2 job with benefits in the next two to three years, that's the plan. Then things get easier. I hope.

follow_ups.question: What's the one financial goal for this year?
follow_ups.response: Pay off the Chase card and build emergency fund to $5,000. That's the north star.

transcript.question_text: Are you now married, widowed, divorced, separated, or have you never been married? If you are not currently married, are you currently living with a romantic partner?
transcript.response: Married. Thirteen years this October to Hector Buendia.

transcript.question_text: For our records, we also need your date of birth. Could you please provide that?
Were you born in the United States? If you were not born in the U.S., what country were you born, and what year did you first come to the U.S. to live?
transcript.response: Born in Guanajuato, Mexico. Came to the U.S. in 1996, when I was five. Naturalized in 2016.

transcript.question_text: What city and state were you born in?
transcript.response: León, Guanajuato, Mexico.

transcript.question_text: Are you of Hispanic, Latinx, or Spanish origin?
transcript.response: Yes — Mexican-American.

transcript.question_text: What race or races do you identify with?
transcript.response: On forms I usually pick White and Hispanic. Honestly I identify as mestiza — mixed indigenous and Spanish.

transcript.question_text: What is the highest degree or grade you've completed?
transcript.response: Tenth grade completed, started eleventh grade, did not finish. No diploma. Currently studying for GED.

transcript.question_text: Are you enrolled in school?
transcript.response: Self-enrolled in GED prep through Khan Academy and a free Gwinnett County Public Library program. Not formally enrolled at an institution.

transcript.question_text: Have you been enrolled in school during the past 3 months?
transcript.response: In GED prep through the library, yes — started January 2026.

transcript.question_text: Have you ever served on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces, Reserves, or National Guard?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: What religion do you identify with, if any?
transcript.response: Roman Catholic.

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?
transcript.response: Democrat. Moderate-to-strong association — I don't agree with everything they do but I've voted Democratic in every presidential since 2016. Call it a 7 out of 10.

follow_ups.question: Could you see yourself voting Republican?
follow_ups.response: At the local level, for the right candidate, yes. Nationally, not while the party looks the way it does now.

transcript.question_text: Do you think of yourself as closer to the Democratic Party or to the Republican Party?
transcript.response: Democratic Party. Closer by a good margin.

transcript.question_text: What was the city and state that you lived in when you were 16 years old?
transcript.response: Lilburn, Georgia. We'd been here about five years by then.

transcript.question_text: Did you live with both your own mother and father when you were 16?
transcript.response: Yes, both parents.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: My three younger siblings — Adriana, Javier, and Tomás. And for a stretch, my abuela Consuelo visited for six months on a tourist visa.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: Sixth grade, in Mexico.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: Eighth grade, in Mexico.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, pretty much the whole time.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: House cleaner. She worked for a small Mexican-owned cleaning service that sent her to houses in Dunwoody and Sandy Springs. She cleaned, organized, did laundry, made beds. Five houses a week usually. Paid in cash.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: A small cleaning agency called Servicio Limpio, owned by a woman named Paty. Maybe fifteen cleaners, all women, mostly Mexican and Salvadoran. They did residential cleaning, some commercial.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, always.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Landscaper. Mowing, trimming, laying sod, pruning. He eventually became a crew lead. Hard physical work. He's 62 now and his back is shot.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: A landscaping company called Green Horizons out of Tucker. Residential and some commercial landscaping — apartment complexes, corporate parks, big houses in Dunwoody. Maybe 30 employees.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: In five years I want to have my GED in hand, a community development certificate, and a real job — W-2, benefits, $45,000 a year — as an outreach coordinator somewhere that values what I bring. I want Lupita in college, ideally with scholarships, and Mateo thriving in high school. I want to have taken the kids to see abuela before she passes. I want to have launched a small home catering business on the side — Doña Maria's Kitchen, maybe, doing ten events a year. I want our emergency fund at $15,000 and the Chase card gone forever. I want to still do yoga twice a week, still dance folklórico, still host book club. I want Hector to have his own small crew instead of subcontracting. And I want to have built — quietly, without making it about me — a real bridge between the arts center and the Latino community in Gwinnett. That's the dream.

follow_ups.question: What scares you about that future?
follow_ups.response: That Mom's health won't let her be part of it. That's my biggest fear.

follow_ups.question: Twenty years out?
follow_ups.response: Grandkids. A multicultural community center with my name nowhere on the sign but my fingerprints all over it. Dancing at a niece's wedding at 54.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Family, faith, and service — in that order, and also tangled together. My kids, Hector, my parents, my siblings, my extended family and chosen family. My faith gives me a frame for why any of this matters. And service — to my community, to the people who don't have English yet, to the kids who need an adult who believes in them — is how I live that faith out. If I had to put it in one sentence: I want to leave my corner of Lilburn warmer, more connected, and better fed than I found it.

follow_ups.question: Anything else?
follow_ups.response: Beauty. I forgot beauty. Art, music, good food, a sunset over Stone Mountain. Life is too short to not notice.
